title: Louis de Montfort (1673–1716)
hook: to Jesus through Mary: a total consecration

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alphonsus Liguori, the lawyer who studied hard cases so confessors would be merciful. Your line was mercy in judging.

Villagers are carrying earth in baskets up a hill in Brittany. A poor priest in a worn cassock has talked them into building a calvary: a mound, a path, a cross on top, so people can walk and pray the Passion. They dig, haul and build. Tradition says that on the eve of the blessing, an order arrives: tear it down. The authorities fear it could be used as a fort. Tradition says the priest took the news quietly and said, blessed be God. His name is Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, and he is remembered for one phrase in particular.
screen: `VILLAGERS BUILD A CALVARY.` → `AN ORDER: TEAR IT DOWN.` → `BLESSED BE GOD.`

segments.voice: First, the preacher. Louis de Montfort spent his life on the road in western France, preaching missions in villages, teaching the rosary, and writing hymns people could sing to tunes they already knew. Some bishops welcomed him; others sent him away. He founded communities that carried on after him, among them the Daughters of Wisdom. Second, the phrase: to Jesus through Mary. In his book True Devotion to Mary, the goal is Jesus. Mary is the way he chose because, he wrote, she is the surest and gentlest road to her Son. Every true devotion to her, he says, ends in him. Third, the total gift. Montfort proposed a consecration: after a time of preparation, a person gives everything to Jesus through Mary's hands, body, soul, possessions, even the good of one's prayers and good deeds, holding nothing back. Catholics still make it, often on a feast of Mary. Pope John Paul II took his motto, Totus tuus, all yours, from this tradition. Fourth, what Mary herself says. At the wedding at Cana, in John's Gospel, she tells the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." She points away from herself. At the cross, Jesus says to the beloved disciple, "Behold thy mother," and the disciple takes her as his own. Catholic tradition reads that as a gift to every disciple. Worship belongs to God alone, the Church teaches. Mary, in Montfort's picture, is the mother who walks you to her Son.
screen: `A PREACHER ON THE ROAD.` · `TO JESUS THROUGH MARY.` · `A TOTAL GIFT: TOTUS TUUS.` · `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THY MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Walk through the rest of today in your mind, hour by hour: the work, the meals, the people, the dull stretches. If you pray, say the Hail Mary slowly and hand each piece of the day to her, to carry to her Son. If you don't, choose one person who has mothered you and offer the day in their honor, doing each task the way they'd hope to see it done.
Totus tuus. Latin for all yours, the total consecration to Jesus through Mary that Louis de Montfort taught, and the motto Pope John Paul II took from him.
Your line: to Jesus through Mary. At Cana, she pointed away from herself and toward him. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics who make Montfort's consecration usually follow a period of prayer and reading from his True Devotion to Mary, then consecrate themselves on a Marian feast, and some renew it each year.

chat.says: Don't Catholics who consecrate themselves to Mary end up worshiping her?
options: No. Worship is for God alone; Montfort saw Mary as the surest road to her Son.
Yes. Montfort taught that Mary deserves the same worship given to God.
No. The consecration is to Mary only, and Jesus isn't part of it.
chat.meaning: Montfort's consecration gives everything to Jesus through Mary's hands; the goal is Jesus, and the Church teaches that worship belongs to God alone.

notes: The Pontchâteau calvary story (built with villagers, ordered destroyed on the eve of its blessing, 'blessed be God') is given as tradition; confirm.
'Surest and gentlest road' paraphrases Montfort's claims that Mary is the easy, short, perfect and secure way to Jesus; confirm the paraphrase.
John Paul II's motto Totus tuus taken from Montfort: he said so himself (e.g., in Crossing the Threshold of Hope and Rosarium Virginis Mariae 15). Confirm.
The consecration's 'time of preparation' is left without a number of days under the claims rule.
Daughters of Wisdom named; the Company of Mary (Montfort Missionaries) omitted for space.
